page: Amazon Web Services r6a.48xlarge is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance running on the AWS Nitro System. It is powered by 3.6 GHz AMD EPYC 7R13 processors on the x86_64 architecture, providing 192 dedicated vCPUs across 96 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading. Memory allocation is scaled to 1536.0 GB of DDR4 memory clocked at 3 GHz, maintaining an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio (8.0 GB per core). Local storage is not bundled, requiring external network-attached storage solutions, and there are no GPUs integrated. Network performance features a baseline throughput of 50 Gbps.

Benchmark testing demonstrates exceptional multi-threaded and memory capacity throughput. In multi-core stress testing, the instance achieved a top-tier stress-ng score of 286,923.87 alongside a PassMark CPU score of 114,312.79. Memory bandwidth reaches 12,140.98 GB/sec in cached small-block reads, and sustains 266.54 GB/sec read and 128.28 GB/sec write throughput under large 256MB blocks. In-memory data store capabilities are underlined by a top-tier 176.67 million operations per second in Redis SET operations, combined with strong database operation scores of 30,194.4 in PassMark suites.

Single-core performance presents a design tradeoff compared to dedicated high-frequency compute alternatives. Single-threaded metrics, including a Geekbench single-core score of 1689.0 and standard compression speeds (29.4 GB/sec in gzip), fall into mid-tier performance bands. Without specialized AVX-512 extensions or discrete GPU acceleration, text generation on larger language models remains modest. However, the density of 192 dedicated cores and 1.5 TB of memory offers substantial cost efficiency for large-scale enterprise workloads that would otherwise require multi-instance clustering.

The r6a.48xlarge instance is ideally fitted for large in-memory databases, distributed caching clusters such as Redis or Memcached, high-throughput database systems, and heavy ETL or data warehousing operations requiring vast RAM capacity alongside wide core parallelism.
